newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish businessmen eye trade under Iraqi oil deal.
newsitem.headline: Turkish businessmen eye trade under Iraqi oil deal.

text.p: Turkish exporters are expected to be among the main beneficiaries of Iraq's "oil-for-food" deal with the U.N., Turkish trade officials said on Wednesday.

But while hopeful that export opportunities will be created by Iraq's sale of $2 billion worth of oil to buy humanitarian supplies, Ankara wants to see a complete end to sanctions on Iraq, which have hit Turkey harder than most.

Trade officials in Ankara say the 1990-91 Gulf Crisis precipitated by Iraq's invasion of Kuwait has cost the Turkish economy $27 billion since 1990. The six-month oil deal will begin to heal this wound, officials said.
"The oil deal will bring trade of around $300 to $500 million. Ultimately the aim is to bring trade up to around $1 billion a year," a Turkish foreign trade official told Reuters.
Turkey's exports to Iraq averaged around $780 million in the five years before the U.N. imposed sanctions on Iraq in 1990 after the invasion.
The official said Turkey's ultimate aim was for sanctions on Iraq, which remain in place, to be lifted. A Turkish columnist echoed this view.
"(Turkey) is hoping the embargo will gradually be lifted and that the trade volume will begin to climb to the levels reached before the Gulf War," liberal Yeni Yuzyil daily columnist Gun Kut said.

The oil-for-food deal does not affect the overall ban on Iraqi oil exports, which cannot be lifted until the U.N. Special Commission says Baghdad has met all weapons requirements under the 1991 Gulf War ceasefire terms.

The trade gains for Turkey from the oil deal are expected to be felt most strongly in Turkey's economically-backward southeast region, where a 12-year-old armed Kurdish insurgency has exacerbated the economy's weakness.

"For the southeast this agreement is of great importance. Agriculture will benefit, so will industry, trade and transport in the area," said Abdulkadir Cikmaz, head of the Southeast Anatolia Exporters' Union (GAIP).

He forecast that Turkey as a whole will take around $400-$500 million of the trade with Iraq, with the southeast region receiving a portion worth around $200-$300 million from the increased sales of foodstuffs and medicines.
Turkish companies have already been selling Iraq basic foodstuffs, mostly wheat flour, pulses and sugar, under U.N. auspices since the sanctions took effect.

Turkish trucks drivers have for years taken food and consumer goods across the border into north Iraq to bring back small amounts of oil in makeshift tankers built under their vehicles in a trade that the Western allies tacitly allow.

Under the $2-billion U.N. deal, Iraq will be able to buy around $1.3 billion worth of medicine, food and other humanitarian supplies. The remaining $700 million raised by oil sales will go towards a U.N. compensation fund and various U.N. operational and administrative costs.

The oil industry specifically will also benefit from the deal. Turkish state-owned pipeline company Botas is expecting to earn around $50 million from transportation fees during the six month period of oil exports.
Turkey's state refiner Tupras said on Wednesday that the U.N. had approved the company's contract with Iraq to buy 75,000 barrels per day of crude oil.
GAIP's Cikmaz shared the view of many Turkish officials that the increased economic opportunities would help to curb the social ills of the southeast region which borders with Iraq.
He said it was essential that the U.N. accord be renewed when it expires in six months to sustain its economic benefits.
